attribution.note: Marcus wrote this in his own co-authored post with Davis, in his own voice, and endorses it.

semantics.note: The claim is a retrospective observation about three approaches. The excerpt names simulation and LLM emergence. Video generation as the third approach is the drafter's reading of the article's structure. That reading is plausible but is not shown in this excerpt.

contract.note: 'Fully satisfactory' has no threshold. The contract reads it as broadly reliable commonsense across ordinary situations, which is a fair and ordinary reading. Because the result turns on that reading and on where each approach's boundary lies, interpretation determines the result.

evidence.note: An ACL 2024 study finds state-of-the-art LLMs perform poorly on spatial reasoning, though they improve with scale. This supports the LLM-emergence part.
A October 2024 benchmark finds that text-to-video models struggle with physical commonsense. This supports the video-generation part.
This is a 2019 PHYRE benchmark result. It does not show the state of simulation approaches by January 2025.
This shows strong simulation-based results on a narrow fluid-physics task. It is restricted progress and neither shows a broad solution nor shows broad failure.

reviews.rationale: The support condition needs evidence of material limits for all three approaches. The packet supports the LLM part (e1) and the video part (e2). For simulation it holds only a 2019 benchmark (e3) and one narrow success (e4), and the packet itself flags this gap. No evidence shows any approach reached broad reliability, so the claim is not contradicted either. The record does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: This is a firm necessity claim ('will require'): if agents work reliably in the real world, they will have common sense. The antecedent is kept. There is no hedge and no deadline.

contract.note: Reading the antecedent as agents completing most realistic end-to-end tasks without human help is fair and ordinary. Whether an agent 'has common sense' is disputed, so interpretation would decide the result if the antecedent were ever met.

evidence.note: In TheAgentCompany v2 (May 2025), the best agent completed 30% of tasks. That is not reliable, so the antecedent was not met then.
On the Remote Labor Index (October 2025), the best agent automated 2.5% of projects. The antecedent was not met as of late 2025.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional with no deadline. The packet's latest verified evidence (October 2025) shows agents were far from reliable, so the antecedent had not occurred. Its status between then and the evaluation date is not verified. When the antecedent did not happen or is unknown, the claim is not scored. The claim stays open.

attribution.note: Marcus asserts this as an 'unsurprising fact' in his own post. The 24% figure comes from the cited paper, but the judgment is his own.

semantics.note: The claim is an observation about the agents tested in TheAgentCompany around its release. The proposition keeps the benchmark basis and the 24% figure.

contract.note: The plain reading is that agents completed only a small minority of realistic workplace tasks and could not stand in for an employee. That is fair and ordinary. A 24% completion rate meets it without stretching.

evidence.note: The v1 abstract (December 2024) reports the best agent completing 24% of tasks, with harder long-horizon tasks out of reach. It is in the target period and on the contract's metric.

reviews.rationale: The contemporaneous TheAgentCompany v1 result shows the best agent completing 24% of tasks, with harder tasks out of reach. That meets the support condition. The authors' 'nuanced' framing notes some success on simpler tasks, but it does not show agents completing most tasks reliably.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post. The Colin Fraser examples are only illustrations.

semantics.note: The claim is an observation that Sora is publicly available and struggles with physical reasoning. Both parts are kept.

contract.note: For a video model, reading 'physical reasoning' as recurring physically implausible output is fair. Counting paid consumer access as public availability is the ordinary reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI's December 9, 2024 announcement records the release to Plus and Pro users after the February preview, and admits the model 'often generates unrealistic physics'. It is a company disclosure, but it is an admission against interest and the contract accepts company disclosures.

reviews.rationale: The release record shows public consumer access by December 9, 2024, about ten months after the February preview. The company's own disclosure admits recurring unrealistic physics in the deployed version. No evidence in the packet shows reliable physical behaviour.
